activities.title: Character sets
activities.description: Ten questions on how text is stored: ASCII, extended ASCII, Unicode and UTF-8, character codes and the arithmetic that goes with them. Written for Leaving Certificate Computer Science.

config.title: Character sets
config.instructions: Each question is worth 1 mark. Where a code is given, use it — you are not expected to have the ASCII table memorised.

questions.stem: Standard ASCII uses 7 bits per character. How many different characters can it represent?
In ASCII the character 'A' has the code 65. What is the ASCII code for 'F'?
In ASCII 'A' is 65 and 'a' is 97. A program converts a capital letter to lower case by adding a fixed number to its code. What is that number?
The digit characters '0' to '9' have the ASCII codes 48 to 57. A program reads the character '7'. What is stored in memory?

options.text: The number 7, ready to be used in arithmetic.
The code 55, which must be converted before it can be used in arithmetic.
The code 7, because ASCII stores digits as themselves.
The code 48, because every digit shares the same code.

questions.stem: Extended ASCII uses 8 bits per character instead of 7. What does the extra bit achieve?

options.text: It doubles the character set to 256 codes, leaving room for accented letters and symbols.
It halves the space each character takes up.
It adds one extra character to the set.
It allows every writing system in the world to be represented.

questions.stem: What problem was Unicode designed to solve?

options.text: Text files were taking up too much disk space.
Computers could not sort text into alphabetical order.
Printers could not reproduce capital letters correctly.
8 bits was not enough to hold the world's writing systems, and rival national character sets disagreed about what each code meant.

questions.stem: UTF-8 is a variable-length encoding. How many bytes does it use to store the letter 'k', which is in the ASCII range?
A program sorts a list of words by comparing their ASCII codes, and puts "Zebra" before "apple". Why?

options.text: Shorter words always sort first.
Every capital letter has a lower ASCII code than every lower-case letter, so 'Z' (90) comes before 'a' (97).
The sort algorithm is broken.
ASCII stores the alphabet in reverse order.

questions.stem: A student saves a plain text file of 500 characters using an encoding that stores every character in one byte. Ignoring any file header, how large is the file?

options.text: 500 bytes
500 bits
4000 bytes
500 kilobytes

questions.stem: Why does it matter that a character set is an agreed public standard rather than something each manufacturer invents?

options.text: Standards make text files smaller.
Standards make computers run faster.
A standard is needed so that text can be encrypted.
Without a shared standard, text written on one system would be read as different characters on another.

q1.explanation: 7 bits give 2^7 = 128 different patterns, so 128 codes, numbered 0 to 127. 127 is the largest code, not the number of them — the count includes 0.

q2.explanation: The capitals are stored in consecutive codes, so 'F' is five letters after 'A': 65 + 5 = 70. Counting the letters on your fingers as A=65, B=66, C=67, D=68, E=69, F=70 is exactly the arithmetic a program does.

q3.explanation: 97 − 65 = 32, and the same gap holds for every letter because both alphabets are stored in consecutive blocks. That is why `chr(ord(letter) + 32)` lower-cases a capital, and it is not a coincidence: 32 is a single bit, so the change is one flip.

q4.explanation: '7' is a character, not a number: it is stored as 48 + 7 = 55. This is why `input()` returns a string that has to be passed through `int()` before you can add anything to it — otherwise Python joins the characters instead of adding the numbers.

q5.explanation: Each extra bit doubles the number of patterns, so 8 bits give 2^8 = 256 codes. Codes 128 to 255 were used for accented letters, box-drawing characters and symbols — but different countries filled them differently, which is precisely the mess Unicode was invented to end.

q6.explanation: Unicode gives every character in every writing system a unique code point, so the same file means the same thing everywhere. Before it, code 233 might be é on one machine and something else entirely on another.

q7.explanation: UTF-8 stores the first 128 code points in a single byte, with exactly the same values as ASCII, and uses two to four bytes only for characters beyond that. That backwards compatibility is why UTF-8 won: an old ASCII file is already a valid UTF-8 file.

q8.explanation: 'Z' is 90 and 'a' is 97, so a straight code comparison puts every capital before every lower-case letter. The sort is doing exactly what it was told; getting dictionary order needs a case-insensitive comparison, such as sorting on `word.lower()`.

q9.explanation: One byte per character × 500 characters = 500 bytes, which is 4000 bits. The answer of 500 bits confuses bits with bytes, and 4000 bytes is the size in bits mislabelled as bytes.

q10.explanation: A character set is an agreement about what each number means. If two systems disagree, the bits transfer perfectly and the message still arrives as nonsense — which is what the infamous garbled-accent problem always was.
